newsitem.title: FRANCE: DUISENBERG SAYS DEFICIT OF 3.2 PCT NO CATASTROPHE.
newsitem.headline: DUISENBERG SAYS DEFICIT OF 3.2 PCT NO CATASTROPHE.

text.p: Dutch central bank president Wim Duisenberg said in an interview with French daily Les Echos that a budget deficit of 3.2 percent would not be a catastrophe for countries wanting to join the euro single currency.

He said a delay in the implementation of the euro could be dangerous for the entire process. Duisenberg expected there to be speculative attacks on the currencies joining the euro in the eight months to January 1, 1999.
It was therefore necessary to give credible indications of the exchange rates between the euro and member currencies from May 1998, he said.
Duisenberg added that he saw the need for coordinating exchange rates between the euro, the dollar and the yen in a sort of group of two or group of three meeting.
The full text of the interview, extracts of which will be published in the Les Echos financial daily on Friday morning, was given to Reuters in advance.
Asked if a delay of the euro would be a catastrophe, Duisenberg said: "I believe that that would be dangerous for the entire project."
He applauded the efforts made by Spain, Portugal and Italy.
"What they have done is remarkable and healthy." he said.
"If the criteria have imposed discipline, a delay in the starting date of the euro, I fear strongly, could lead to the evaporation of that (discipline)."
Duisenberg is a candidate for the presidency of the European Central Bank and will succeed Alexandre Lamfalussy as the head of the European Monetary Institute (EMI) in July.
On the budget deficit criterion in the Maastricht Treaty, Duisenberg said: "The Treaty leaves a certain place open to a interpretation of the criteria. The text is about a trend at medium term.
"The criteria do not have a scientific value. In mathematics, between 2.9 and 3.2 is rounded off to three. I want to underline again that viability is more important than decimals."
